sm: The episode opens with headlines and the news. Democrats are celebrating a historic midterm win, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries calling it an American tsunami. President Trump congratulated Democrats, said he would work with them unless they are destructive, blamed consumer price hikes from the Iran war as a likely factor, and said he has no regrets about acting against Iran. Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the minority leader post, while Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan are both running for it. Senate counts in Mississippi and Alaska were still too close to call, with an Alaska controversy over a second candidate named Dan Sullivan, whom Republicans call decoy Dan. The report also covers ballot measures on school sports, Vice President Vance's comments about changing ties with Israel, and Israel's own election fallout.

Reporter Harrison Waters says Democrats are laying out an agenda that includes reversing Medicaid work requirements, blocking tariffs, and passing a bill to stop the war with Iran. Former ambassador Ryan Crocker says Democrats now have unprecedented leverage through the budget, and Senator Chris Murphy argues that Congress must be able to see war up close and that the American military presence in the Middle East worsens tensions. Congress has until December eleventh to pass spending bills or another stopgap, and Republicans keep control until January third. Analyst Ahmad Sharawi expects investigations of the Pentagon and pressure for a negotiated settlement as gas prices stay high. Then Hunter Baker joins the hosts, and they replay his March comment that the Strait of Hormuz and pain at the pump would hurt Trump. Baker says that anyone could have predicted heavy midterm losses from high gas prices and a Middle East conflict.

Hunter Baker says the blame for the midterm losses comes down to Trump, because he called the play and was overconfident after his 2024 win. The hosts say Republicans look bleak as Trump becomes a lame duck, so they turn to the Democrats. Baker warns that Democrats would squander their advantage by going on a Trump hunt of subpoenas and investigations, and says voters want bills that actually improve things. He says Democrats should avoid woke discourse, court packing, and statehood for D.C. and Puerto Rico, and that a competent nominee like Josh Shapiro would be hard to beat in 2028. After sponsor messages, Lauren Smith reports on de-banking, starting with Steve Curtis of Timothy 2 Project International, whose Bank of America accounts were closed with three weeks' notice and no explanation. David Cox of Family Council describes a similar case with the payment processor WePay.

Cox says WePay labeled Family Council a high risk organization, and Bank of America told Curtis it was because of business in Cuba, though he says the ministry follows federal trade rules. Regulators had required banks to avoid reputational risk, but those rules were rolled back this year. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency reviewed nearly one hundred thousand complaints from 2020 to 2025 and reported in October that banks discriminated based on religious and social views. Lawyer Caleb Dalton calls the evidence damning, and the report says one bank turned away groups from both sides for being partisan. Without unredacted documents, legal action is hard, and six states have fair access laws. A short item follows about a Pennsylvania man who set a Guinness record by seeing 1,207 movies in a year. Then Kristen Flavin begins a story on composer Stephen Limbaugh, who is writing a symphony for America's 250th birthday, inspired by Dvorak, Copland and John Williams.

Limbaugh says he wants to be the next iteration of the American musical tradition and treats the symphony as a meditation on what is American, not a linear history. He has raised sixty thousand dollars through crowdfunding to record it, three movements are done, and the fourth is mapped out but not orchestrated. The recording with a live orchestra is set for early January, and the premiere will be at Belmont University in Nashville before next July. Commentator Daniel Darling then reflects on the election from Texas, where Democrats won the governor's race. He calls it a major setback for Christian conservatives but says they should not despair or withdraw from citizenship. He cites Chuck Colson that politics is not the church's first calling and says Christian hope rests in Christ's reign, closing with Psalm ninety and Psalm 116.
